nature-pol-205.title: Subsidies: paying people to do more of something
nature-pol-205.text: Many governments spend several percentage points of their GDP on subsidies, year after year. A subsidy is government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses, to support them or to encourage some activity. The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations. Subsidies come in many shapes. Some are direct spending, such as the payments governments may hand out in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity. Others are {{ref:nature-pol-237}}, cheap loans, price support, or goods and services the government provides. Some do clear environmental good. Governments that subsidize rail and bus transport cut congestion and pollution compared with cars. But the tool cuts both ways. Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences, a theme that runs through this chapter.

nature-pol-194.title: Extended producer responsibility: makers pay for the waste
nature-pol-194.text: In a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry, Thomas Lindhqvist first formally put forward a simple idea: make manufacturers pay for what becomes of their products. Extended producer responsibility, or EPR, holds producers responsible for environmental costs across a product's whole life cycle, mainly the cost of dealing with it as waste. The logic is that brand owners control product design, so they are best placed to cut toxicity and waste. Producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products. EPR can take the form of programs for reuse, buyback or {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products. Unlike {{ref:nature-eecon-034}}, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of recycling into the product price and relieves local governments. The deposit-refund system is described as based on its principles. In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%. A drawback is the administrative burden of rules that differ between countries and waste streams.

nature-pol-208.title: Perverse subsidies: support that harms twice over
nature-pol-208.text: In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion in agricultural subsidies, and EU farmers $47 billion. Farm subsidies like these often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and {{ref:nature-res-027}}. Perverse subsidies are those whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment. A subsidy rarely starts out perverse. It can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal. Perverse subsidies drain budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health. They cause resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor. And they are hard to remove, because they become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia.

nature-pol-224.title: Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power
nature-pol-224.text: As of 2019, more than 50 countries had feed-in tariff policies. A feed-in tariff speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply. It usually guarantees access to the grid and pays prices based on generating costs. Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts. Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power. A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in tariffs the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity. They have a cost. Funded by a surcharge on bills, they added 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017. Yet renewables can also lower spot market prices through the {{ref:nature-clim-125}}, as happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.

nature-pol-232.title: Pollution registers: the public's right to know
nature-pol-232.text: After the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to know about toxic chemicals, several countries set up pollutant release and transfer registers. These systems collect and publish information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities. The aim is to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions. A protocol to the {{ref:nature-gov-126}} requires its parties to set up such registers. That 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them. The registers have a limit. Their data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

nature-pol-218.title: Environmental certification: choosing to be checked
nature-pol-218.text: Environmental certification is a voluntary form of environmental regulation. A company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service. Most such services have a logo, commonly called an ecolabel, that certified products can carry. It is seen as a form of {{ref:nature-gov-067}}, letting firms reduce environmental harm by following external, measured objectives. Companies take it up to sell ethical products, improve their image, get on better with stakeholders and earn more profit. Independent checks of their green claims can also shield them from accusations of {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}. The whole system rests on demand. It only works if there are consumers willing to buy the resulting green products, and consumers may be willing to pay extra for ethically produced goods.

nature-pol-229.title: ISO 14000: international standards for environmental management
nature-pol-229.text: As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries. The ISO 14000 family is a set of international standards for {{ref:nature-gov-100}}, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in March 1996. The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws and keep improving. Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself. ISO 14001 is the core standard. It sets out a framework for an environmental management system but no required level of environmental performance. The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself. Firms that adopt it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs, and may gain a competitive advantage. Its predecessor was BS 7750, published in 1992 as the world's first environmental management system standard.

nature-pol-211.title: Forest certification: a label for responsibly managed wood
nature-pol-211.text: About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program. Forest certification is a voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard. An independent body writes the standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it. Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests, pioneered third-party certification in the early 1990s. With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners now offer certification. The two largest are the FSC and the PEFC, which covers about two-thirds of certified forest area. Critics such as Greenpeace and Jared Diamond question the rigor of rival standards, which some say logging companies set up to confuse consumers. The schemes defend their standards. Demand comes from publishers' paper commitments, green buying by governments, green building standards and laws against {{ref:nature-res-139}}.

nature-pol-226.title: Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries
nature-pol-226.text: German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004. Green industrial policy is government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting {{ref:nature-found-045}} and moving toward a {{ref:nature-clim-208}}. The case rests on hard beginnings. Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable. New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones, because of {{ref:nature-pol-038}}, so governments nurture technological niches. Without government intervention, the market is unlikely to move to a low-carbon economy on its own. Subsidies for a targeted sector are the most common form. Other tools include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green buying by governments.

nature-pol-231.title: The Inflation Reduction Act: America's biggest climate law
nature-pol-231.text: The Inflation Reduction Act, a 2022 United States law, is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy. According to the CBO and JCT, it invests $783 billion in {{ref:nature-clim-114}} and climate provisions. Consumers get 10 years of tax credits for heat pumps, rooftop solar and efficient electric heating and cooling. It also created a $27 billion {{ref:nature-clim-091}}, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, to finance smaller regional green banks. After the act, Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels.

nature-pol-203.title: Rio Principle 15: the precautionary approach
nature-pol-203.text: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration says that where serious or irreversible damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures. This precautionary approach is a softer form of the {{ref:nature-pol-201}}, one that takes local capabilities and costs into account. Even the label is contested. The United States has opposed the word 'principle' in negotiations, because a principle of law is a source of law. The line between the two terms is described as diffuse and sometimes controversial. The {{ref:nature-gov-044}} builds on the approach of Principle 15.

nature-pol-202.title: Strong and weak precaution
nature-pol-202.text: Buying a smoke detector or wearing a seatbelt is weak precaution, and people practice it daily. Weak versions of the precautionary principle only permit action without full proof. They allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay. Strong precaution requires regulation whenever harm is possible, even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high. This 'no-regrets' stance ignores cost. The 1982 UN {{ref:nature-gov-056}} gave the strong version its first international recognition.

nature-pol-189.title: Ecolabels as regulation without the state
nature-pol-189.text: At the 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, countries agreed to bring environmental issues into manufacturing and to steer consumption toward {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Ecolabeling fits that aim. It is a self-regulating, market-based tool that partly takes over from government {{ref:nature-pol-147}}. The standards are voluntary, but they put market pressure on large companies to adopt greener production. In this way ecolabeling has become a form of non-state authority, at national and international levels.

nature-pol-235.title: Green public procurement: governments buying green
nature-pol-235.text: Rules can steer public bodies to buy efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and renewable energy. That is green public procurement, the part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals. It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve {{ref:nature-eecon-191}} and grow the market for greener products, which can drive green innovation. It relies heavily on {{ref:nature-eecon-029}}, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.

nature-pol-196.title: Making electronics makers pay for e-waste
nature-pol-196.text: E-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash, contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium. All are dangerous to health and the environment. Producer responsibility rules tackle it by making producers pay for its {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}. That may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}, products built to wear out early. Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them. Whether it really speeds greener design is disputed.

nature-pol-219.title: What environmental certification cannot do
nature-pol-219.text: Usually only the best-performing operators get certified, so firms with no interest in environmental management stay outside. That is the first limit of voluntary certification. The second is cost. Suppliers usually bear it, and the extra profit often does not cover it. Many certification costs are fixed, so large producers gain an advantage over small ones through economies of scale. The third is reach. Tropical deforestation usually comes from converting forest to other uses, which lies outside {{ref:nature-res-092}} certification.

nature-pol-234.title: Sustainable procurement: buying for the whole life cycle
nature-pol-234.text: Public spending averages 12% of GDP in OECD countries and up to 30% in developing countries, which gives governments enormous purchasing power. Firms have similar clout: purchases can exceed 50% of a company's expenses, and over 80% in retail, electronics and cars. Sustainable procurement puts that power to work. It means buying goods, services and works that give value for money over the whole life cycle ({{ref:nature-acct-050}}). The purchases should also be benefit society and stay within the environment's limits. Procurement has traditionally weighed only price and quality; the sustainable kind adds the third-party effects of buying decisions. It favors renewable or recycled materials and less waste, and checks suppliers for pollution or harm to habitats. It need not cost more. Sustainable options often cost about the same, and even pricier ones can save money through lower energy, water and waste costs over their life.

nature-pol-187.title: Three types of environmental label
nature-pol-187.text: The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types, by what they cover and how strictly they are checked. Type I (ISO 14024) is a voluntary label based on many criteria, checked by an independent third party that looks at a product's life cycle impacts. Type II (ISO 14021) is a claim a manufacturer or retailer makes about itself, without third-party auditing. Type III (ISO/TR 14025) declares measured life cycle data. It does not rate the product but helps buyers compare. 'Type I-like' labels cover a single issue, such as a pass/fail energy limit for appliances.

nature-pol-198.title: Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ
nature-pol-198.text: In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition. The dispute is over definitions. Estimates add up government payments, compare domestic prices with world prices, and sometimes count health and climate damage. Counting unpriced damage makes IMF estimates far larger than those using OECD and International Energy Agency definitions. One IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies, at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%. The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.

nature-pol-223.title: Does fair trade help the farmers?
nature-pol-223.text: One estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee. Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries. A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero, because of an oversupply of certification. Economists add a market argument. Coffee demand is highly inelastic, barely responding to price ({{ref:nature-econ-358}}), so more fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers. Yet a study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found fair trade meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.
